why_in_two_sentences: Our page answers the query with a mechanism-level account (the read-and-adjust loop, the two-house origin, and explicit fawn-versus-pleasing and fawn-versus-freeze distinctions) that goes far past both competitors' generic sign lists. PsyPost and Healthline win only on a few composition and trust elements, so the gap is about surfacing coverage we lack rather than depth.
what_the_winner_does_that_we_dont: Attribute the term to psychotherapist Pete Walker in or near the opening answer, which both competitors do and our answer-box omits.

Frame the fawn response inside a compact all-four-responses set (fight, flight, freeze, fawn) with a one-line gloss of each, giving searchers the taxonomy up front the way PsyPost's overview list and Healthline's structured sections do.
Name the physiological layer explicitly (cortisol and adrenaline release, autonomic nervous system activation) as Healthline does, instead of describing racing heart and tight chest only in prose.

Add a short standalone signs-of-fawning list (difficulty saying no, over-apologizing, taking responsibility for others' emotions, lack of boundaries, chameleon-like adapting) as a scannable block, matching PsyPost's bulleted 'Common Behaviors' section.
Cover hybrid trauma responses (for example fawn-flight or flight-freeze) as a named subsection, which Healthline includes and our freeze section only partially touches.
Add an attachment-style origin angle as its own labeled section, the way Healthline ties childhood caregiver bonds to which response gets stuck.
what_we_do_that_they_dont: Separate threat-driven fawning from approval-driven people-pleasing in a full side-by-side comparison table (aim, historical cost, body state, triggers, what it responds to), where PsyPost only offers one FAQ paragraph on the difference.
Explain the pre-conscious timing (the read-and-adjust loop completing before you get a vote), which neither competitor addresses.
Distinguish fawning from freezing and note they need different first moves, absent from both pages.
Provide an above-the-fold identify-box of verbatim internal sentences readers can match word-for-word, a self-recognition device neither competitor has.
Front-load a safety/scope section routing at-risk readers to domestic-violence services and clinicians before any technique.
Cover the 'nobody ever hit anybody' volatile-mood household as an origin path, beyond the abuse/neglect framing both competitors default to.

above_the_fold.ours: A reader sees an H1 matching the query, a boxed 'short answer' defining fawn as the fourth response that moves toward threat, then an identify-box of verbatim internal sentences and a seminar link; it earns the next scroll by naming the exact experience and promising why standard advice missed it.
above_the_fold.theirs: PsyPost opens with a tight definition that credits Pete Walker and immediately positions fawn within the four trauma responses, so a searcher gets both the definition and the taxonomy before scrolling.
above_the_fold.gap: Add the Pete Walker attribution and a one-line fight/flight/freeze/fawn framing inside or directly under the answer-box so the fold delivers the definition, the source, and the taxonomy at once.

trust_signals: Healthline carries a named author, a byline date, and a medically-reviewed-by credential while PsyPost cites Pete Walker as originator, whereas our page leans on specificity and mechanism but surfaces no author, review, or named-source attribution to the reader.
one_change_with_most_traffic_impact: Add Pete Walker attribution plus a one-line fight/flight/freeze/fawn taxonomy into the above-the-fold answer-box, matching the definitional and source cues both ranking competitors put first.
